name: Pamona (Retired)
world_status: statement found in a copy we already had

new_statements.quote: Men behoeft in 't B. nooit in 't onzekere te verkeeren omtrent de plaats van den klemtoon. De geklemtoonde lettergreep is altoos duidelijk van de andere syllaben te onderscheiden. […] De grondwoorden, die in het B. nooit minder dan twee lettergrepen tellen, hebben den klemtoon op de voorlaatste syllabe. Zoo hebben pela „huid", oeë „water", ga'a „scheiden", toedja „stampen" den klemtoon op pe, oe, ga, toe […]. (p. 23) […] Voorvoegsels kunnen nimmer den klemtoon veranderen. (p. 24)
new_statements.translation: In B[are'e] one need never be in doubt about the place of the stress. The stressed syllable is always clearly distinguishable from the other syllables. […] The root words, which in B. never have fewer than two syllables, have the stress on the penultimate syllable. Thus pela 'skin', oeë 'water', ga'a 'separate', toedja 'pound' have the stress on pe, oe, ga, toe […]. (p. 23) […] Prefixes can never change the stress. (p. 24)
new_statements.citation: Adriani, N. 1931. Spraakkunst der Bare'e-taal. Verhandelingen van het Koninklijk Bataviaasch Genootschap van Kunsten en Wetenschappen 70. Bandoeng: A. C. Nix.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the root (grondwoord) and stays there under affixation: prefixes never move it, most suffixes and the enclitics mo, pa, dja do not move it either (inekoe 'my mother' stressed on i = ine + koe; koepampopokaoe stressed on the root kaoe), so relative to the word edge stress can sit on the antepenult or further left. Only the bisyllabic suffix -aka takes primary stress on its own penult (nakitasáka), and the fossilized suffixes -a/-ani, -o/-oni and the old postposed article e shifted stress one syllable to the right (sompóa < sompo). The paragogic final syllable -i that preserves an original final consonant does not count for stress (kóbati < kobat, lindoegi < lindoeg). Stress is realized as a rise in voice/pitch on the stressed syllable rather than force, and unstressed syllables are not reduced.
new_statements.secondary_stress: p. 24: one would expect words with 3–5 prefixes to carry a main and a secondary stress (on the pa- syllables), but usually the voice simply rises slowly to the stressed syllable, lengthens it slightly, and falls; with the suffix -aka the root's original stress is kept as a secondary stress (bijtoon), e.g. tetendelaka, nakitasaka, koedongesaka.
new_statements.exceptions: Roots whose last syllable repeats the previous vowel (pronounced as a double-length vowel: kia, nee, dii, loo, koeoe) — the accent spreads over the whole long vowel but 'can safely be said' to fall on the first part (p. 23). Suffix -sa sometimes shifts stress one place rightward, sometimes not (kampóresa ~ kamporésa; p. 25). Dialect exceptions: the Todjo dialect and the To Pada (Peleroe, Londi, Lembo nTonara) move stress to the penult of a suffixed or encliticized word, attributed to Buginese and Mori influence (anánja vs. B. ánanja; p. 8 with footnote). The Ampana dialect shifts stress only with the suffixes -a and -aka (Adriani 1900, tr. Mead 2014, orig. p. 542).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, citation forms of roots and derived words; Adriani contrasts B. stress (rise in voice/pitch, no reduction of unstressed syllables) with Dutch dynamic stress. Source-language-wise this describes Bare'e = Pamona proper [pmf, pamo1252], Poso/Lake Poso standard dialect.
new_statements.identity_note: pamo1255 is not a language: it is Glottolog's Bookkeeping node for the retired ISO 639-3 code [bcx] 'Pamona', which ISO CR 2007-199 (Mead, adopted 2008-01-14) split into Pamona [pmf] = pamo1252 and Batui [zbt] = batu1260 after establishing that Batui ('Baha') is a Saluan-Banggai language wrongly listed as a Pamona dialect since Adriani 1914. The stress statement quoted here describes Bare'e = Pamona proper (pamo1252), which already has a catalog row (classification excluded, no first-hand quote); the quote should be lodged under pamo1252, not under this retired key. The Batui half is a separate check target (batu1260, own folder); Mead & Pasanda 2015 give penultimate, non-phonemic stress for the Saluan/Batui wordlists (pp. 29–30). Dialect caveat: Adriani 1931 p. 8 reports that the Todjo dialect (Glottolog poso1239 area) and the To Pada (topa1242) move stress to the penult of suffixed words.

sources.note: Ampana dialect section (orig. pp. 542–543): 'Stress falls in the same place as in Bare'e, on the next-to-last syllable of the stem. Only the suffixes -a and -aka cause stress to shift to the next-to-last syllable of the word compounded therewith, for example kámba, kambaráka.. ndoróa'; with -kaku the stem stress becomes secondary (ikakáku). Bobongko (p. 440–441): stress on the penult of each word, shifting with suffixes; prefixes do not affect accent.
